title: Linux PrivEsc Explorer
description: Searchable Linux privilege escalation assessment techniques for authorised security testing.

techniques.name: sudo Permissions
techniques.summary: Enumerate commands the current account is permitted to execute through sudo and assess whether the delegation crosses an unintended privilege boundary.
found: The current user has one or more sudo rules.
The delegated command may execute as root or another privileged account.
requires: The current user must have an applicable sudo rule.
The delegated functionality must provide more privilege than intended for practical escalation.
validation: Record the exact sudo rule, target user, executable, and permitted arguments.
Determine whether NOPASSWD, SETENV, wildcards, editors, interpreters, shell functionality, plugins, or writable dependencies are involved.
Prefer configuration evidence before executing privileged functionality.
detection: Monitor sudo authentication and execution events.
remediation: Delegate only the commands required for the user's role.
Restrict arguments where practical.
Avoid delegating unrestricted shells, interpreters, editors, or highly flexible utilities.
Protect all scripts and configuration consumed by delegated commands.

techniques.name: sudo NOPASSWD Delegation
techniques.summary: A sudo rule using NOPASSWD permits execution of the delegated command without re-entering the user's password.
found: sudo -l reports a NOPASSWD rule.
The user can invoke the specified command without interactive password authentication.
requires: An applicable NOPASSWD rule.
The delegated command must expose functionality capable of crossing the intended privilege boundary.
validation: Identify the exact target identity and delegated executable.
Determine whether the command itself is intended administrative access or whether it exposes unintended functionality.
Check the delegated binary against its official documentation and GTFOBins where applicable.
detection: Audit NOPASSWD entries in sudoers configuration.
Monitor execution of high-risk delegated commands.
remediation: Remove unnecessary NOPASSWD rules.
Use narrowly scoped commands and arguments.
Do not rely on password prompting as the only control if the delegated executable itself is unsafe.

techniques.name: sudo SETENV
techniques.summary: SETENV can permit environment-variable control for a delegated sudo command and may become security-sensitive when the executable trusts environment-controlled behaviour.
found: sudo -l reports SETENV for a delegated command.
requires: An applicable SETENV sudo rule.
The delegated program must consume a security-sensitive environment setting.
validation: Identify which environment variables the delegated application accepts.
Review library, module, configuration, interpreter, and PATH behaviour.
Confirm actual environment handling rather than assuming dangerous variables are preserved.
detection: Monitor changes to sudo environment policy.
remediation: Remove SETENV where it is unnecessary.
Use controlled environment values for privileged commands.
Avoid privileged applications that load user-controlled modules or configuration.

techniques.name: sudo Wildcard Rule
techniques.summary: Wildcards in sudo rules can provide broader argument control than intended depending on how sudo and the delegated program interpret the command line.
found: A sudoers rule contains wildcard-controlled arguments.
requires: The wildcard must permit attacker-controlled argument expansion or equivalent unintended functionality.
The delegated program must interpret that control in a security-sensitive way.
validation: Record the exact sudo rule.
Determine which arguments the wildcard can match.
Review the delegated application's argument parser and option handling.
Do not assume every wildcard rule is exploitable.
detection: Audit sudoers rules for wildcard use.
Review high-privilege delegated commands after sudoers changes.
remediation: Avoid broad wildcards in privileged rules.
Use explicit commands and tightly constrained arguments.
Use wrapper programs only when the wrapper itself validates input safely.

techniques.name: GTFOBins sudo Candidate
techniques.summary: A sudo-delegated binary appears in GTFOBins and exposes functionality that may be relevant to privilege-boundary analysis.
found: A delegated binary has a documented GTFOBins sudo function.
requires: The exact sudo configuration must satisfy the documented conditions.
The functionality must provide unintended privilege beyond the approved delegation.
validation: Compare the exact binary and sudo rule with the GTFOBins entry.
Confirm version and command restrictions.
Treat GTFOBins as a reference, not proof of exploitability.
detection: Audit sudo rules granting access to highly flexible utilities.
Monitor privileged use of unusual administrative binaries.
remediation: Remove unnecessary sudo access.
Use purpose-built administrative interfaces rather than general-purpose utilities where possible.
Restrict arguments and environment.

techniques.name: SUID Binary Enumeration
techniques.summary: Identify executables carrying the SUID permission bit and determine whether their elevated effective UID creates an unsafe privilege boundary.
found: One or more SUID executables are accessible to the current user.
requires: The SUID executable must run with a more privileged effective UID.
Its functionality must permit unintended privileged behaviour.
validation: Compare discovered binaries with the expected operating-system baseline.
Prioritise custom, unusual, legacy, copied, or unexpectedly located SUID binaries.
Inspect ownership and permissions before active testing.
detection: Alert on unexpected SUID-bit creation or changes.
Use file-integrity monitoring for privileged executable locations.
remediation: Remove unnecessary SUID bits.
Remove obsolete privileged executables.
Use narrower privilege mechanisms where appropriate.
Protect privileged executable files and directories.

techniques.name: Custom SUID Binary
techniques.summary: A custom or organisation-specific executable carries SUID and should be reviewed for unsafe command execution, environment trust, file handling, and input processing.
found: A non-standard executable carries the SUID bit.
The file is owned by root or another privileged identity.
requires: The current user can execute the binary.
A security-sensitive implementation weakness must be present.
validation: Review command execution and absolute versus relative paths.
Review environment-variable handling.
Review writable configuration and dependencies.
Review temporary-file and symlink handling.
Review user-controlled input before active validation.
detection: Perform secure code review of custom privileged applications.
remediation: Remove SUID where unnecessary.
Apply least privilege.
Use absolute paths and controlled environments.
Drop privileges as early as possible.
Protect configuration, dependencies, and temporary resources.

techniques.name: SGID Binary Enumeration
techniques.summary: Identify SGID executables and determine whether their effective group identity grants access to privileged resources.
found: One or more SGID executables are present.
requires: The effective group must provide security-sensitive access.
The executable must expose functionality capable of abusing that access.
validation: Identify the file group.
Determine what resources the group can access.
Prioritise unusual and custom SGID executables.
detection: Maintain an inventory of SGID executables.
remediation: Remove unnecessary SGID permissions.
Restrict privileged group access.
Protect privileged binaries and their dependencies.

techniques.name: File Capability Enumeration
techniques.summary: Enumerate Linux file capabilities and identify executables granted fine-grained privileges beyond normal Unix permissions.
found: One or more files have Linux capabilities assigned.
requires: The capability must provide security-sensitive functionality.
The executable must expose a way to use that capability beyond its intended purpose.
validation: Record the executable and exact capability set.
Review the binary's functionality.
Determine whether namespaces or security controls restrict practical impact.
detection: Maintain a baseline of file capabilities.
Monitor setcap and capability extended-attribute changes.
remediation: Remove unnecessary capabilities.
Assign only the minimum required capabilities.
Avoid granting broad capabilities to interpreters and general-purpose utilities.

techniques.name: CAP_SETUID
techniques.summary: CAP_SETUID can permit manipulation of process user identities and is particularly sensitive when assigned to flexible user-accessible executables.
found: A user-accessible executable has CAP_SETUID.
requires: The capability must be effective in the relevant context.
The executable must expose functionality capable of changing UID in a security-sensitive manner.
validation: Confirm the exact capability flags.
Review the executable's documented UID-related functionality.
Consider namespaces and NoNewPrivileges.
detection: Alert on CAP_SETUID assignment to unexpected executables.
remediation: Remove CAP_SETUID unless explicitly required.
Avoid assigning CAP_SETUID to interpreters or general-purpose utilities.
Use dedicated narrowly scoped privileged helpers.

techniques.name: CAP_SETGID
techniques.summary: CAP_SETGID can permit manipulation of group identity and may expose resources protected by privileged group membership.
found: A user-accessible executable has CAP_SETGID.
requires: The executable must permit useful group-identity manipulation.
The resulting group must provide additional security-sensitive access.
validation: Identify the exact capability flags.
Determine which privileged groups matter on the host.
Review application behaviour before active testing.
remediation: Remove unnecessary CAP_SETGID capabilities.
Use narrowly scoped service identities and permissions.

techniques.name: CAP_DAC_OVERRIDE
techniques.summary: CAP_DAC_OVERRIDE can bypass selected discretionary access-control checks and may expose protected files through a capable executable.
found: An accessible executable has CAP_DAC_OVERRIDE.
requires: The executable must expose file operations relevant to the protected resource.
validation: Identify which file operations the application permits.
Use metadata and controlled test files before accessing real secrets.
Consider additional LSM restrictions.
detection: Monitor unexpected access to sensitive files.
remediation: Remove unnecessary CAP_DAC_OVERRIDE.
Use a narrower capability or application-specific privilege design.

techniques.name: CAP_DAC_READ_SEARCH
techniques.summary: CAP_DAC_READ_SEARCH can bypass selected file-read and directory-search permission checks.
found: An accessible executable has CAP_DAC_READ_SEARCH.
requires: The executable must expose read or traversal functionality useful against protected resources.
validation: Review the executable's file-access features.
Avoid reading unrelated sensitive files when permission evidence is sufficient.
remediation: Remove unnecessary CAP_DAC_READ_SEARCH.
Use least privilege for file-reading services.

techniques.name: CAP_SYS_ADMIN
techniques.summary: CAP_SYS_ADMIN covers a broad set of privileged operations and can significantly weaken privilege boundaries when exposed to untrusted users or containers.
found: The process or an accessible executable has CAP_SYS_ADMIN.
requires: The capability must apply in a namespace where the relevant privileged operation has security impact.
validation: Determine whether the capability exists on the host or only inside a namespace.
Review mount, namespace, filesystem, and application context.
Avoid invasive mount or namespace manipulation where configuration evidence is sufficient.
remediation: Avoid CAP_SYS_ADMIN unless strictly required.
Drop unnecessary container capabilities.
Use narrowly scoped capabilities.

techniques.name: CAP_SYS_PTRACE
techniques.summary: CAP_SYS_PTRACE can permit tracing of otherwise protected processes under applicable namespace and security-policy conditions.
found: A process or accessible executable has CAP_SYS_PTRACE.
requires: A security-sensitive target process must be traceable.
Yama, namespaces, LSM policy, and process protections must permit the operation.
validation: Review ptrace restrictions.
Identify the namespace relationship.
Do not attach to critical production processes merely to prove capability.
remediation: Remove unnecessary CAP_SYS_PTRACE.
Apply Yama and least-privilege process isolation where appropriate.

techniques.name: CAP_SYS_MODULE
techniques.summary: CAP_SYS_MODULE permits kernel module management and represents a highly privileged capability.
found: The current context or an accessible executable has CAP_SYS_MODULE.
requires: The capability must apply to the relevant kernel namespace and module operations must be available.
validation: Confirm the capability context.
Configuration evidence is generally sufficient to demonstrate excessive privilege.
Do not load a kernel module solely to prove impact.
remediation: Remove CAP_SYS_MODULE from untrusted workloads.
Restrict kernel module operations to trusted administrative contexts.

techniques.name: Root Process Enumeration
techniques.summary: Identify root processes and determine whether they trust resources controlled by the current user.
found: One or more privileged processes are running.
requires: A privileged process must consume a lower-privileged controlled resource or expose unsafe functionality.
validation: Identify executable paths and configuration.
Review scripts, plugins, working directories, environment files, sockets, and writable dependencies.
remediation: Run services as dedicated unprivileged identities where possible.
Protect privileged process dependencies.

techniques.name: systemd Service Enumeration
techniques.summary: Review systemd services for privileged execution paths and lower-privileged writable dependencies.
found: One or more systemd services execute privileged commands.
requires: A lower-privileged user must control a trusted service resource for practical escalation.
validation: Record User, Group, ExecStart, ExecStartPre, ExecStartPost, EnvironmentFile, and WorkingDirectory where relevant.
Check file and parent-directory permissions for trusted resources.
detection: Maintain file-integrity monitoring for service resources.
remediation: Run services using dedicated least-privilege accounts.
Protect unit files, executables, scripts, configuration, and environment files.
Apply appropriate systemd hardening options.

techniques.name: Writable Root Service Script
techniques.summary: A lower-privileged user can modify a script executed by a service running as root or another privileged identity.
found: A privileged service executes a script writable by the current user or one of the user's groups.
requires: The privileged service must execute the writable script.
The service must run with higher privilege than the current user.
validation: Confirm the service execution identity.
Confirm the script path used by the service.
Confirm effective write access through Unix permissions or ACLs.
The privilege relationship can normally be demonstrated without changing the script.
detection: Monitor modifications to scripts executed by privileged services.
Monitor service restarts and privileged process creation.
remediation: Remove lower-privileged write access.
Correct ownership and ACLs.
Protect all parent directories.
Separate writable application data from privileged executable content.

techniques.name: Writable Privileged Service Executable
techniques.summary: A lower-privileged account can modify or replace an executable launched by a privileged service.
found: A privileged service executable is writable or replaceable by a lower-privileged user.
requires: The service must execute the affected file.
The service must run with higher privilege.
validation: Confirm effective write or replacement rights.
Check parent-directory permissions.
Do not replace production binaries merely to demonstrate impact.
detection: Monitor package and service binary changes.
remediation: Restrict executable and directory write permissions.
Use trusted package-managed locations where appropriate.
Run services with minimum required privilege.

techniques.name: Writable systemd Unit
techniques.summary: A lower-privileged user can modify a systemd unit that controls privileged service execution.
found: A privileged unit file is writable by the current user or an accessible group.
requires: The unit must be loaded or otherwise used by systemd.
The affected service must execute with greater privilege.
validation: Confirm effective write access.
Confirm the service execution identity.
Do not edit the unit solely to prove the condition.
detection: Monitor /etc/systemd/system and relevant vendor unit directories.
Alert on unexpected daemon-reload and unit changes.
remediation: Restrict unit-file write access to administrators.
Protect parent directories.
Review custom service deployment processes.

techniques.name: Writable systemd EnvironmentFile
techniques.summary: A privileged service consumes an environment file that is writable by a lower-privileged account.
found: A service references EnvironmentFile and the file is lower-privileged writable.
requires: The service must consume a variable whose value influences security-sensitive behaviour.
validation: Identify the variables consumed by the service.
Determine whether they influence executable paths, arguments, libraries, configuration, or other privileged behaviour.
detection: Monitor privileged service environment files for changes.
remediation: Restrict write access to privileged environment files.
Avoid using lower-trust configuration for privileged command construction.

techniques.name: systemd Timer Enumeration
techniques.summary: Enumerate systemd timers and inspect the corresponding services for privileged scheduled execution.
found: One or more systemd timers execute recurring services.
requires: The corresponding privileged service must trust a lower-privileged controlled resource for escalation.
validation: Map each interesting timer to its service.
Identify execution identity and writable dependencies.
detection: Monitor timer and corresponding service-unit changes.
remediation: Protect scheduled service resources.
Run scheduled workloads with minimum required privilege.

techniques.name: Cron Job Enumeration
techniques.summary: Review cron configuration for privileged scheduled jobs and user-controlled dependencies.
found: System or user cron jobs are configured.
requires: A privileged scheduled command must trust a resource controlled by the current user for escalation.
validation: Record the execution user, command, schedule, PATH, scripts, and dependencies.
Check file and directory permissions.
detection: Alert on unexpected root cron changes.
remediation: Protect cron files and scripts.
Use absolute command paths.
Run scheduled tasks with least privilege.

techniques.name: Writable Root Cron Script
techniques.summary: A script executed by a root cron job is writable or replaceable by a lower-privileged user.
found: A root cron job executes a lower-privileged writable script.
requires: The cron job must execute as root or another higher-privileged identity.
The current user must have effective modification or replacement rights.
validation: Confirm the scheduled execution identity.
Confirm the exact script path.
Confirm effective write or replacement access.
Avoid changing the script where configuration evidence proves the boundary.
detection: Monitor privileged cron scripts for modification.
Monitor cron configuration and root scheduled process execution.
remediation: Remove lower-privileged write access.
Correct ownership and ACLs.
Protect parent directories.

techniques.name: Privileged Cron PATH Trust
techniques.summary: A privileged scheduled job executes a relative command and searches a PATH containing a directory controlled by a lower-privileged user.
found: A privileged scheduled command uses a relative executable name.
An earlier PATH directory may be writable by the current user.
requires: The privileged job must use the affected PATH.
The command must be resolved through PATH.
A lower-privileged writable directory must precede the intended executable.
validation: Confirm the exact PATH in the scheduled context.
Confirm the command is invoked without an absolute path.
Confirm effective directory write access.
detection: Review privileged scripts for relative command execution.
Monitor changes to privileged job PATH configuration.
remediation: Use absolute executable paths.
Use a controlled root-owned PATH.
Remove untrusted writable directories from privileged execution paths.

mitre.name: PATH Environment Variable Path Interception by PATH Environment Variable

techniques.name: Privileged PATH Hijack Candidate
techniques.summary: A privileged process or script executes a relative command while using a PATH containing a lower-privileged writable directory.
found: A privileged consumer invokes an executable by relative name.
The effective PATH contains a potentially writable directory.
requires: The privileged process must resolve the command through PATH.
The current user must control an earlier search directory.
validation: Establish the PATH used by the privileged consumer rather than relying only on the current shell PATH.
Confirm directory write access.
Confirm command resolution order.
detection: Review privileged scripts for relative command execution.
remediation: Use absolute executable paths in privileged scripts.
Use controlled PATH values.
Remove lower-privileged writable directories from privileged PATHs.

mitre.name: PATH Environment Variable Path Interception by PATH Environment Variable

techniques.name: World-Writable File Enumeration
techniques.summary: Identify world-writable files and determine whether any are trusted by privileged processes.
found: One or more world-writable files exist.
requires: A privileged consumer must trust or execute the writable file for escalation.
validation: Identify ownership and purpose.
Determine whether a privileged process executes, loads, or trusts the file.
Do not report ordinary writable data files as privilege escalation findings.
detection: Baseline privileged directories for unexpected world-writable files.
remediation: Remove unnecessary world-write permissions.
Separate writable data from privileged executable or configuration content.

mitre.name: Linux and Mac File and Directory Permissions Modification

techniques.name: World-Writable Directory Enumeration
techniques.summary: Identify world-writable directories and determine whether they allow replacement or introduction of resources trusted by privileged processes.
found: One or more world-writable directories exist.
requires: A privileged process must consume content from the directory in a security-sensitive way.
validation: Check sticky-bit semantics.
Identify privileged consumers.
Determine whether file creation, replacement, or deletion creates practical influence.
detection: Monitor privileged application directories for permission changes.
remediation: Remove unnecessary world-write permissions.
Use the sticky bit where appropriate for shared temporary directories.
Protect privileged application directories.

mitre.name: Linux and Mac File and Directory Permissions Modification

techniques.name: Unexpected POSIX ACL
techniques.summary: POSIX ACLs can grant access beyond traditional owner, group, and other permission bits.
found: A security-sensitive resource has additional ACL entries.
requires: The ACL must grant the current user or group security-sensitive access.
The resource must influence a privileged consumer.
validation: Identify effective ACL permissions.
Consider ACL masks.
Map the accessible resource to its privileged consumer.
remediation: Remove unnecessary ACL entries.
Use least privilege and documented administrative groups.

mitre.name: Linux and Mac File and Directory Permissions Modification

techniques.name: Writable Parent Directory
techniques.summary: A protected privileged file may still be replaceable when a lower-privileged user controls a parent directory.
found: A parent directory in the path to a privileged resource is writable.
requires: Directory permissions must permit practical replacement or manipulation of the trusted resource.
A privileged consumer must use the affected path.
validation: Review each path component.
Consider sticky bit and ownership semantics.
Confirm whether the resource can actually be replaced.
detection: Audit parent directories of privileged executables and configuration.
remediation: Restrict parent-directory write access.
Use root-owned trusted deployment paths.

mitre.name: Linux and Mac File and Directory Permissions Modification

techniques.name: Credentials in Shell History
techniques.summary: Shell history can expose passwords, tokens, connection strings, or administrative commands containing reusable credentials.
found: History files contain credential-related commands or strings.
requires: The exposed secret must remain valid and provide access to a more privileged identity or resource for escalation.
validation: Minimise secret exposure.
Determine the associated account or service.
Do not display complete secrets in reports.
detection: Monitor secret scanning results in administrative environments.
Review operational procedures that place secrets on command lines.
remediation: Rotate exposed credentials.
Use secret-management mechanisms.
Avoid secrets in command-line arguments and shell history.

techniques.name: Credentials in Environment Variables
techniques.summary: Environment variables may expose application passwords, API tokens, cloud credentials, or service secrets.
found: Credential-related environment-variable names or values are visible.
requires: The secret must provide additional authorised access or higher privilege.
validation: Search variable names before displaying values.
Determine whether the secret is valid and security-sensitive without unnecessary disclosure.
detection: Review service configuration for plaintext environment secrets.
remediation: Move secrets to an appropriate secret-management mechanism.
Restrict process and environment exposure.
Rotate exposed credentials.

techniques.name: Accessible SSH Private Key
techniques.summary: An accessible SSH private key may permit authentication as another local or remote identity.
found: An SSH private-key file is readable by the current user.
requires: The key must correspond to an account or system in assessment scope.
The key must provide additional access beyond the current identity.
validation: Record metadata without printing private-key content.
Identify the likely account and authorised destination.
Handle private keys as sensitive evidence.
remediation: Correct private-key permissions.
Rotate compromised keys.
Use passphrases and managed SSH credentials where appropriate.

techniques.name: Application Configuration Credentials
techniques.summary: Application configuration may contain reusable database, service, cloud, API, or administrative credentials.
found: A readable application configuration appears to contain credential material.
requires: The credential must remain valid.
The credential must provide higher privilege or access relevant to the assessment.
validation: Target known applications instead of dumping entire filesystems.
Record file path and permission evidence.
Redact secret values.
detection: Monitor access to high-value configuration files.
remediation: Remove plaintext secrets where possible.
Restrict configuration-file permissions.
Rotate exposed secrets.
Use dedicated service accounts and secret-management systems.

techniques.name: docker Group Membership
techniques.summary: Access to a rootful Docker daemon can represent a host-equivalent administrative boundary because the daemon controls containers and host resources.
found: The current user belongs to the docker group or otherwise has Docker socket access.
requires: The accessible daemon must provide security-sensitive host control.
The daemon must not be limited by an authorization mechanism that prevents the relevant operations.
validation: Confirm socket access.
Determine whether the daemon is rootful or rootless.
Review authorization plugins and daemon configuration.
Do not launch a privileged host-mounted container merely to prove the relationship.
detection: Audit membership of the docker group.
Monitor Docker API and container creation activity.
remediation: Restrict Docker daemon access to trusted administrators.
Use rootless Docker where appropriate.
Apply daemon authorization controls where required.

techniques.name: Accessible Docker Socket
techniques.summary: A user-accessible Docker API socket may provide extensive control over a rootful Docker daemon and host resources.
found: /var/run/docker.sock or another Docker API endpoint is accessible.
requires: The daemon must permit security-sensitive operations.
The daemon's host privilege must exceed the current user's privilege.
validation: Identify socket owner and group.
Determine daemon privilege model.
Review authorization controls.
Use metadata and daemon information before any active container creation.
detection: Monitor container creation and host mount activity.
remediation: Restrict socket permissions.
Do not expose the Docker API to untrusted identities.
Use rootless Docker where suitable.

techniques.name: LXD Administrative Access
techniques.summary: LXD administration can provide significant control over containers and host-backed resources depending on daemon configuration.
found: The current user appears to have LXD administrative access.
requires: The daemon must operate with privileges capable of exposing host resources.
The user must be permitted to perform security-sensitive container operations.
validation: Confirm the installed LXD model and daemon privilege.
Review storage pools, devices, profiles, and host-resource exposure.
Avoid creating host-mounted privileged containers merely to prove impact.
detection: Monitor container and device configuration changes.
remediation: Restrict LXD administration to trusted users.
Apply least privilege to container management.

techniques.name: disk Group Membership
techniques.summary: The disk group can provide direct block-device access on many Linux systems, bypassing normal filesystem-level permissions.
found: The current user belongs to disk or has equivalent block-device access.
requires: Relevant host block devices must be accessible through the granted permissions.
validation: Record group membership and device permissions.
Do not read raw production disks merely to demonstrate impact.
detection: Audit membership of the disk group.
Monitor raw block-device access where supported.
remediation: Restrict disk-group membership to trusted administrators.
Use narrowly scoped mechanisms for applications requiring device access.

techniques.name: shadow File Access
techniques.summary: Access to /etc/shadow exposes local password hashes and may weaken account security even when it does not directly provide root execution.
found: The current user or one of its groups can read /etc/shadow.
requires: The access must exceed what is intended for the user's role.
validation: Use permission evidence rather than copying password hashes.
Determine whether the access is intentionally delegated.
remediation: Restrict /etc/shadow access.
Remove unnecessary shadow-group membership.

techniques.name: Privileged Log Access
techniques.summary: Membership in groups such as adm or systemd-journal may expose sensitive operational logs containing credentials, tokens, or administrative data.
found: The current user has elevated log-reading access.
requires: The logs must contain security-sensitive information that provides additional privilege or access.
validation: Review only the minimum log data required.
Do not classify log access itself as root escalation without an additional security-sensitive condition.
detection: Prevent secrets from being written to logs.
remediation: Restrict sensitive log access.
Remove credentials and tokens from application logs.

techniques.name: libvirt Administrative Access
techniques.summary: Virtualisation management access may provide control over virtual machines, storage, devices, and host-backed resources.
found: The current user appears to have libvirt or equivalent virtualisation-management access.
requires: The available daemon operations must expose security-sensitive host resources.
validation: Review daemon privilege and socket permissions.
Review storage pools and host-backed device access.
Avoid modifying production virtual machines merely to demonstrate administrative capability.
detection: Monitor VM, storage, and device configuration changes.
remediation: Restrict virtualisation administration to trusted users.
Separate administrative roles where feasible.

techniques.name: Privileged Unix Socket
techniques.summary: A Unix-domain socket accessible to the current user may expose an administrative API implemented by a more privileged daemon.
found: A socket is accessible to the current user.
The associated daemon may run with greater privilege.
requires: The socket protocol must expose security-sensitive operations.
The daemon must not independently reject the current identity.
validation: Identify the server process.
Record socket ownership and permissions.
Review documented API methods and authentication.
detection: Monitor access to privileged administrative sockets where feasible.
remediation: Restrict administrative socket access.
Apply application-level authentication and authorization.
Run daemons with least privilege.

techniques.name: Privileged D-Bus Service
techniques.summary: A privileged D-Bus service may expose methods whose authorization should be reviewed for unsafe local privilege boundaries.
found: Privileged services are exposed on D-Bus.
requires: A security-sensitive method must be callable by the current identity.
D-Bus policy and any Polkit checks must permit the operation.
validation: Identify the service owner.
Review exported methods.
Review D-Bus and Polkit authorization.
Do not invoke destructive administrative methods.
detection: Monitor privileged D-Bus method use where supported.
remediation: Apply explicit authorization to privileged methods.
Restrict custom system-bus services.

techniques.name: Polkit Authorization Review
techniques.summary: Custom or overly broad Polkit rules can permit lower-privileged users to invoke security-sensitive operations through privileged services.
found: Polkit rules or privileged Polkit-integrated services are present.
requires: A rule or service authorization decision must grant unintended privileged functionality.
validation: Review custom rules first.
Identify permitted users and groups.
Map each rule to the affected privileged action.
remediation: Use least-privilege Polkit rules.
Avoid broad group-based administrative authorization.
Remove obsolete custom rules.

techniques.name: NFS no_root_squash
techniques.summary: An NFS export using no_root_squash can preserve remote root ownership semantics and may create a local privilege boundary issue depending on export access and filesystem use.
found: An NFS export appears to use no_root_squash.
requires: The tester must have authorised access to an allowed NFS client context.
The exported filesystem must interact with privileged execution or sensitive host resources.
validation: Record the export path and allowed clients.
Review root_squash settings.
Review mount options and the role of files stored on the export.
Avoid creating privileged executable content on production exports merely to prove impact.
remediation: Use root_squash unless no_root_squash is explicitly required.
Restrict NFS clients.
Separate writable exports from privileged executable locations.

techniques.name: Filesystem Mount Security Options
techniques.summary: Mount options such as nosuid, noexec, nodev, ro, and rw can materially change the exploitability of filesystem-based privilege escalation candidates.
found: A filesystem relevant to a candidate has security-relevant mount options.
requires: A separate privilege escalation candidate must depend on the affected filesystem behaviour.
validation: Record the exact mount point and options.
Use mount configuration to refine exploitability rather than reporting missing options automatically.
remediation: Use nosuid, nodev, noexec, or read-only mounts where appropriate to the workload.
Do not apply restrictive mount options without considering application requirements.

techniques.name: Writable Privileged Library
techniques.summary: A privileged executable loads a dynamic library that a lower-privileged user can modify or replace.
found: A library loaded by a privileged consumer is writable or replaceable.
requires: The privileged process must load the affected library.
The current user must have effective modification or replacement rights.
validation: Confirm the actual library path.
Confirm privileged execution context.
Confirm effective write access.
Avoid modifying production shared libraries.
detection: File-integrity monitoring for privileged library directories.
remediation: Restrict library and directory write permissions.
